occupation.note: 'Augustin Taylor, builder, still living in Chicago, arrived June, 1833' - and Andreas's account of St Mary's calls him the architect and builder of the church: 'Augustine D. Taylor was the architect' of the twenty-five by thirty-five foot building whose lumber came by scow from St Joseph at $12 per thousand.

persons.note: AN ARRIVAL WITH A MONTH, WHICH ONLY SIX HOUSEHOLDS IN THIS PARCEL HAVE. He is also the man whose name is attached in the Chicago literature to the first balloon-frame building - St Mary's - and this record makes no claim about that, because Andreas calls him the architect and says nothing about the framing method. HE IS IN THE DATASET BECAUSE THE 1835 TOWN CANNOT BE BUILT WITHOUT HIS TRADE. Andreas's roster is the only list this project holds that names artisans at all, and every name on it is a documented alternative to an inferred one.

research_note: A CARPENTER IN THE YEAR THE TOWN NEEDED CARPENTERS MOST, and one of two Taylor brothers in this parcel - Anson H. Taylor hauled the lumber for the same church with his own team and has his own household. THE OCCUPATION FIELD UNDERSTATES HIM: Andreas calls him a builder and an architect and this project's vocabulary records the trade he worked in. A dedicated 'builder' value exists in the vocabulary and is used for men described only that way; carpenter is chosen here because it is what he was.

kin.note: AUGUSTINE DEODAT TAYLOR AND ANSON H. TAYLOR ARE BROTHERS. The Chicago History Museum's encyclopedia entry on church architecture distinguishes the builder of St Mary's from 'brother Anson who hauled lumber', and this parcel already carried that sentence in prose without ever writing it as a link. Graded inferred: the corpus holds this project's summary of the encyclopedia rather than a quoted page. Five Taylor households stand here; the source names Anson, so the tie reaches one. Ruled under T-0865; the sentence was rescued from a proposal to delete it as unsourced (PR #948).

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry.

address_later.value: res Michigan ave, bet Lake and Randolph
address_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 prints this address against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Taylor, Augustine Deodat, carpenter and builder, res Michigan ave, bet Lake and Randolph [died March 31, 1891, aged 94-11-3.]'. It is evidence about 1843, written here as 1843's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.

back_projection.note: NOT READ BACK, BECAUSE SOMETHING BETTER ALREADY STANDS. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 prints an address against this name in 1843, and it is left where it is. An 1835 placement already stands: this household works at `st_marys_church`, and clause 2 says an attested 1835 placement always beats a door printed 8 years later. The later address stays on the record as 1843's evidence and moves nothing.

residence_back_projection.note: REFUSED, AND THE REFUSAL IS THE RECORD. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 prints where this man lived in 1843 and this pass will not carry it back to 1835. Michigan Avenue is the lakefront street south of the river and is NOT the 1835 layer's Michigan Street, which runs east from La Salle on the north side. Two streets, one word, and the 1839 directory prints both. A refusal is written here rather than dropped so that a later run can see the address was read and ruled on, not missed (docs/RESIDENCE-BACK-PROJECTION.md, clause R4).
